memoryText: The blood shall be a sign for you, on the houses where you are. And when I see the blood, I will pass over you, and no plague will befall you to destroy you.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read Exodus 12:13 slowly, several times, and then say it from memory. Read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone you trust.
memoryVerseMeditation:
Exodus 12:13 is the gospel in one sentence. It was spoken on the night before the exodus, and it says everything about how God saves.

“The blood shall be a sign for you.” The blood was a sign for the people inside the house, not for God. It was the thing that gave them confidence that the judgment would not touch them. They did not have to feel safe. They had a sign. When you are afraid, the promise is not that you will feel better, but that there is a sign: the blood.

“When I see the blood.” It is God who sees the blood, and the sight of it is what determines what he does. Notice what is not said. God does not say, “When I see your goodness” or “When I see your repentance.” He says, “When I see the blood.” The ground of your safety is not what is in you but what is on the door. A lamb has died in your place.

“I will pass over you.” This is the great promise. Judgment is real, and it falls on Egypt. But those under the blood are safe. The word “pass over” is related to a Hebrew verb that means to hover protectively, like a bird over its nest (Isaiah 31:5). God does not just skip the house. He guards it.

“And no plague will befall you to destroy you.” The protection is complete.

For the Christian, the blood is the blood of Christ. “Since, therefore, we have now been justified by his blood, much more shall we be saved by him from the wrath of God” (Romans 5:9). There is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). Every time you doubt whether you are safe, return to this verse.
weekInReview: This week you read the story of the plagues and the exodus. You watched Moses go to Pharaoh and make things worse, and you heard God answer his complaint with the promise to bring out, deliver, redeem, and take. You read the plagues of frogs, gnats, flies, livestock, boils, and hail, and saw how Pharaoh gave way and hardened his heart again and again. You watched Pharaoh bargain, and Moses refuse to leave a hoof behind. You read the instructions for the Passover and heard God say, “When I see the blood, I will pass over you.” Then you walked through the Red Sea on dry ground and saw the waters close over Pharaoh’s army. In Psalm 106, you read a confession of Israel’s later unfaithfulness, and the one word that rescues the story: “Nevertheless.” The week taught that salvation is God’s work, secured by the blood of a substitute.
reflectionQuestions: Pharaoh bargained with God, offering part but not all. What part of your life do you tend to hold back from God? What would it look like to say, “Not a hoof shall be left behind”?

How does the Passover lamb help you understand what Jesus did on the cross? Think about the details: without blemish, its blood applied, protection from judgment. What does it mean for you personally that Christ is your Passover lamb?
Moses told Israel at the sea, “The LORD will fight for you, and you have only to be silent.” What battle are you trying to fight on your own? What would it look like to be silent and let God fight?
prayerPrompts: Thank God that when he sees the blood, he passes over you.
Ask him to fight for you, and rest in him.
Tell him what you are tempted to trust apart from Christ.
